entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Audomar, known posthumously as Saint Omer, was a pivotal figure in the Christianization of the Morini and other Germanic tribes inhabiting the coastal regions of what is now northern France and Belgium during the 7th century. Appointed Bishop of Thérouanne around 639 CE by King Dagobert I of the Franks, Audomar played a crucial role in consolidating Merovingian authority and extending the reach of the nascent Frankish church into formerly pagan territories. His episcopate, spanning over three decades until his death in 670 CE, laid foundational spiritual and administrative structures that profoundly influenced the religious and social landscape of early medieval Artois and Flanders, establishing monastic centers and converting local populations. His work was part of a broader wave of monastic and missionary expansion in Neustria and Austrasia.

Born into a noble family in La Haye-Traversaine, near Coutances, Neustria, Audomar initially pursued a monastic life at Luxeuil Abbey under the renowned Abbot Eustace. After his episcopal appointment, Audomar established his see in Thérouanne, a strategically important Roman-era town. He actively recruited missionaries, notably Bertin, Momelin, and Ebertram, from Luxeuil to assist in his evangelistic efforts. Together, they founded the monastery of Sithiu (later Saint-Bertin Abbey) around 649 CE on the banks of the Aa River, which became a powerful center for the propagation of Christianity and a significant economic hub in the region. Audomar's pastoral work involved direct engagement with local populations, often through the destruction of pagan shrines and the construction of new churches.
